values.description: A replica may be demoted from preferred service without being treated as permanently failed.

values.label: RPC failover health telemetry
values.description: Failover behavior supplies server-health telemetry used in replica failure assessment.

clusters.name: Client Feature Default Policy
clusters.description: Which client features run by default in foreground, background, or disabled modes?

relations.reading: Choices on Client Feature Default Policy affect the outcomes of Working-Directory Change Detection
relations.rationale: Disabling or backgrounding client status features changes interactive filesystem-change detection behavior and latency.

values.label: Compatibility-oriented disabling of foreground features
values.description: Advanced foreground Git work is disabled by default to preserve compatibility and avoid blocking interactive commands.

values.label: Background execution of client maintenance
values.description: Client maintenance and metadata generation run asynchronously rather than during interactive operations.

clusters.name: WAL Object-Storage Tier
clusters.description: Which object-storage performance tier supports the write-ahead log's durability and ingestion rate?

relations.reading: Choices on WAL Object-Storage Tier affect the outcomes of Reference Update Performance
relations.rationale: The documents tie object-storage PUT latency and tier selection directly to WAL ingestion and push throughput.

values.label: S3 Standard WAL storage tier
values.description: Standard object storage provides durable WAL storage for moderate push ingestion rates.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone WAL storage tier
values.description: A lower-latency object-storage tier supports higher WAL ingestion rates.

iterations.explanation:
Consolidated 192 draft values across 31 dimensions (merge threshold 0.350, borderline band 0.400). Merged 1 near-duplicate value:
  - [Repository Placement and Routing] "Relational database for repository-location tracking" → "External repository-routing database"
The remaining 190 values were distinct enough to keep as generated.
Evidence linking: 331 of 339 open codes assigned to a value (similarity >= 0.50); 48 of 48 documents now support at least one value.

clusters.name: Replication Mechanism
clusters.description: Which mechanism carries repository updates between replicas, from Git-aware and packfile methods to gossip or asynchronous propagation?

relations.reading: Choices on Replication Mechanism affect the outcomes of Repository Consistency Guarantee
relations.rationale: Replication mechanisms determine whether replicas can remain fully synchronized and what complexity and failure behavior the consistency model entails.

values.label: Git application-level replication
values.description: Replicate repositories through application-level Git operations, optionally combined with rsync for scalable synchronization and repair.

values.label: Packfile-level replication
values.description: Replication operates on Git packfiles while leaving Git itself undistributed.

values.label: Filesystem block-level replication
values.description: Replication copies filesystem blocks as the older architecture.

values.label: Git system distribution
values.description: Git is distributed as a system-level component requiring maintenance of a suitable fork.

values.label: Optimistic UDP gossip replication
values.description: Replicas exchange WAL metadata through lossy UDP gossip and independently validate durable state.

values.label: Asynchronous packfile distribution
values.description: Large pushed packfiles distribute without consensus because unreachable objects need not be synchronized immediately.

values.label: Whole-packfile local caching
values.description: Caching complete packfiles locally can make random access acceptable but does not scale across very many repositories.

clusters.name: Repository Distribution Architecture
clusters.description: How are repository copies exposed, distributed, and fanned out across hosting infrastructure?

values.label: Proxy-mediated replica distribution
values.description: A proxy accepts client pushes and distributes updates to multiple fileservers.

values.label: Filesystem-level repository distribution
values.description: The filesystem containing Git data is distributed while the application remains unchanged.

values.label: Packfile-level repository distribution
values.description: Packfiles rather than the whole filesystem are distributed among repository-serving locations.

values.label: NFS-backed repository distribution
values.description: A network filesystem such as NFS provides distributed storage for centralized repositories.

values.label: RPC-based repository access
values.description: Applications access repositories through RPC while repositories remain on dedicated fileservers.

values.label: Multi-server repository replication
values.description: Each repository has copies on multiple servers for resilience and distributed serving.

values.label: Orchestrated push fan-out
values.description: An orchestrator distributes pushed packfiles to repository replicas.

values.label: Network-filesystem correctness and performance problems
values.description: Networked filesystem semantics can make Git operations slow and buggy because Git assumes local-disk behavior.

values.label: Durable highly available repository access
values.description: Preserve repository access and durability despite server and network failures through replicated storage.

values.label: Central-server stress reduction
values.description: Proxy caching reduces repeated object-serving work handled by the central server.

clusters.name: Repository Consistency Guarantee
clusters.description: Which freshness, consistency, and partition-priority guarantee do repository replicas provide?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Consistency Guarantee limit the options available on Replica Placement
relations.rationale: Read routing must account for replica freshness when replicas are geographically dispersed; stale replicas cannot serve reads requiring current repository state.

values.label: Fully synchronized repository replicas
values.description: All replicas maintain current repository state so clients and CI can immediately observe updates.

values.label: Eventually consistent repository views
values.description: Replicas may temporarily omit newly pushed commits, creating unreliable client and CI behavior.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition priority
values.description: Prioritize consistency and partition tolerance over availability when replication or communication failures occur.

values.label: Immediate post-push commit visibility
values.description: Reliable visibility of newly pushed commits is the operational result of strong synchronization.

values.label: Full-consistency implementation complexity
values.description: Maintaining complete synchronization imposes substantial implementation complexity.

values.label: Globally consistent reads across replicas
values.description: Replication and durable-state validation provide a consistent repository view across replicas.

clusters.name: Replica Consistency Enforcement
clusters.description: Which read-validation or catch-up mechanism enforces the selected repository consistency guarantee?

values.label: ETag-validated replica reads
values.description: Conditional object-store validation checks replica freshness before serving reads.

values.label: Read-time replica catch-up
values.description: A replica catches up from durable storage when validation detects a newer WAL index.

clusters.name: Replica Placement
clusters.description: Where are repository replicas deployed relative to geography and network proximity?

relations.reading: Choices on Replica Placement affect the outcomes of Repository Failure Transition
relations.rationale: Distributing reads across replicas and excluding unavailable hosts enables maintenance without interrupting new reads or losing service capacity.

values.label: Geographically dispersed replica placement
values.description: Replicas span separated datacenters or geographic areas for disaster survivability and closer user access.

values.label: Low-latency replica proximity
values.description: Replicas remain relatively close to the proxy to satisfy communication-latency requirements.

values.label: Co-located fileserver replicas
values.description: Replicas are kept adjacent to one another to satisfy latency-sensitive block replication.

values.label: Rack-separated replica placement
values.description: Place repository replicas in distinct racks treated as availability zones to withstand rack-wide failures.

clusters.name: Replica Read Routing
clusters.description: How are replicas selected for reads and assigned voting or non-voting participation?

values.label: Freshness-aware nearest-replica routing
values.description: Reads use the nearest replica that has been assessed as up to date.

values.label: Non-voting geographic replicas
values.description: Geographic replicas serve reads without being required for push quorum, preserving write availability during reachability failures.

values.label: Single-replica read routing
values.description: Reads route to any one up-to-date replica without cross-replica read coordination.

values.label: Improved geographic transfer speed
values.description: Users near replicas experience faster Git transfers as a result of geographic, freshness-aware read serving.

values.label: Linear read scaling through replication
values.description: Adding replicas increases read throughput approximately linearly without reducing push throughput.

clusters.name: Repository Failure Transition
clusters.description: Which failure and recovery behavior governs repository access when a server crashes or becomes unavailable?

relations.reading: Repository Failure Transition requires Maintenance Execution Mode to be decided first
relations.rationale: Safe server retirement depends on knowing how ongoing maintenance and repository operations are scheduled and executed.

values.label: Crash-recovery maintenance logic
values.description: Planned maintenance reuses recovery mechanisms designed for crashes and permanent failures.

values.label: Immediate server reboot or unplugging
values.description: Abrupt retirement interrupts long-running reads and can discard their progress.

values.label: Interrupted long-running reads
values.description: Direct reboot can force large clones and other reads to restart elsewhere, losing prior progress.

clusters.name: Server Reboot Maintenance Policy
clusters.description: How are servers drained, rebooted, and concurrency-limited during planned maintenance?

values.label: Quiescing before reboot
values.description: The server drains active operations before shutdown and stops accepting new reads.

values.label: Rolling reboot maintenance
values.description: Perform maintenance through sequential server or rack reboots while preserving service availability.

values.label: Random server reboot testing
values.description: Randomly reboot file servers to test failure handling while production reads may be active.

values.label: Bounded reboot concurrency
values.description: Limit the number of servers rebooted concurrently within a maintenance zone to preserve redundancy and service access.

clusters.name: Repository Integrity Verification
clusters.description: Which checksum strategy verifies repository integrity efficiently during operation and recovery?

values.label: Continuous repository checksumming
values.description: Repository copies are continually checksummed to detect corruption and unhealthy on-disk state.

values.label: Incremental repository checksum maintenance
values.description: Maintain replica-state checksums incrementally from prior state and changed references.

values.label: From-scratch repository checksum recomputation
values.description: Recompute a replica checksum from the complete reference list after each update.

values.label: XOR reference-pair checksum aggregation
values.description: Aggregate reference-name/value hashes with XOR so changed references can be removed and replaced incrementally.

values.label: Localized failure-detection false positives
values.description: Confine an incorrect server-level failure conclusion to the detecting application server without disrupting production traffic.

values.label: Rapid corruption-recovery requirement
values.description: Corruption detection and repair must be rapid to preserve push availability when replicas are authoritative.

clusters.name: Write Continuity During Maintenance
clusters.description: How do replication and quorum choices preserve writes during server maintenance?

values.label: Continued write replication during quiescing
values.description: Writes continue reaching the quiescing replica so it does not fall arbitrarily behind.

values.label: Replica-tolerant write quorum
values.description: Remaining replicas can continue an in-progress write when one rebooting replica drops out.

clusters.name: Maintenance Execution Mode
clusters.description: How and when is repository maintenance initiated, run, blocked, or disabled by operators?

relations.reading: Choices on Maintenance Execution Mode affect the outcomes of Working-Tree Population Mode
relations.rationale: Maintenance choices such as background cleanup and fetch scheduling change client-side repository performance and the practicality of large working trees.

values.label: Background maintenance through registration
values.description: Registered repositories receive automatic configuration, fetching, commit-graph, and cleanup operations.

values.label: Foreground operator-controlled maintenance
values.description: Operators invoke maintenance on demand or according to their own schedule.

values.label: Single-command maintenance execution
values.description: One command runs the repository’s configuration, fetching, commit-graph, and cleanup tasks together.

values.label: Periodic foreground garbage collection
values.description: The client periodically performs foreground garbage collection despite the impracticality for very large repositories.

values.label: Command-triggered synchronous garbage collection
values.description: User-facing Git commands synchronously invoke complete automatic object-data rewrites.

values.label: Maintenance opt-out controls
values.description: Allow operators to pause or unregister repositories from background maintenance.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Incremental maintenance reduces thousands of packs and large storage footprints to substantially smaller repositories.

values.label: Foreground command blocking
values.description: Large synchronous maintenance operations delay simple interactive Git commands.

values.label: Maintenance resource exhaustion
values.description: Complete repository rewrites can consume CPU and memory and stall the client system.

values.label: Performance decay without automatic collection
values.description: Disabling automatic collection avoids synchronous cost but allows accumulated objects to degrade Git performance.

values.label: Git command acceleration
values.description: Improve interactive Git command performance as the result of repository registration and maintenance.

clusters.name: Maintenance Compaction Strategy
clusters.description: Which compaction and obsolete-pack expiration strategy manages repository storage during maintenance?

values.label: Incremental geometric compaction
values.description: Maintenance incrementally compacts packfiles geometrically before a full repack is needed.

values.label: Small-pack batch repacking
values.description: Maintenance rewrites bounded batches of small packs instead of rewriting all repository data at once.

values.label: Deferred obsolete-pack expiration
values.description: Obsolete packs remain until no multi-pack-index references remain, allowing concurrent Git commands to continue.

values.label: Two-phase repack and expiration
values.description: Replacement-pack creation and indexing are separated from deletion of unreferenced packs.

clusters.name: Maintenance Scheduling Policy
clusters.description: How are bookkeeping and user updates prioritized, coalesced, and delayed during maintenance?

values.label: Bookkeeping-update coalescing
values.description: Cascading bookkeeping reference changes are combined into fewer transactions.

values.label: User-update priority scheduling
values.description: User-initiated reference updates receive priority over non-time-critical bookkeeping work.

values.label: Bookkeeping-update processing delay
values.description: Large bookkeeping cascades can keep repositories busy and delay or time out user updates.

clusters.name: Working-Tree Population Mode
clusters.description: Which population model controls the files and objects materialized in a client working tree?

relations.reading: Choices on Working-Tree Population Mode limit the options available on Working-Directory Change Detection
relations.rationale: The populated-tree strategy determines which paths need monitoring and whether a watcher can avoid scanning irrelevant directories.

values.label: Sparse-checkout population
values.description: Only selected repository paths are populated, scaling working-tree size through Git-native mechanisms.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem population
values.description: A virtual filesystem defers populated-size costs and presents repository content through virtualization.

values.label: Partial-clone GVFS integration
values.description: GVFS interaction is implemented through Git’s partial-clone interface so both mechanisms reinforce one another.

values.label: Full working-directory population
values.description: The client materializes the complete working directory instead of using sparse population.

values.label: Checkout performance bottleneck
values.description: Moving from virtualization to sparse-checkout makes checkout slower than with the former virtual filesystem.

values.label: Populated-file modification detection cost
values.description: Detecting modifications across populated files becomes expensive as the working set grows.

values.label: Higher file-population cost than index adjustment
values.description: Materializing files requires substantially more data handling than adjusting index entries.

values.label: Reduced Git working-tree management burden
values.description: Selective population and separated outputs reduce the work required to manage the working tree.

clusters.name: Client Repository Integration
clusters.description: Which client and protocol integration supplies large-repository capabilities through Git, GVFS, or custom distribution?

values.label: Co-located GVFS cache server
values.description: A cache server near sufficiently large repositories supports GVFS requests for large user groups.

values.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
values.description: GVFS deployment proceeds without the cache-server infrastructure required for scalable operation.

values.label: Git protocol with Scalar registration
values.description: Existing Git-protocol repositories use Scalar registration when GVFS cache infrastructure cannot be resourced.

values.label: Custom Git client distribution
values.description: Distribute a custom Git client containing repository-scaling features.

values.label: Core Git feature integration
values.description: Contribute scaling features to core Git to remove the custom-client requirement.

values.label: GVFS protocol in standard Git client
values.description: Expose the GVFS protocol as the standard Git client's large-repository transfer mechanism.

clusters.name: Repository and Build Placement
clusters.description: How are the repository, source tree, and build outputs arranged on the client filesystem?

values.label: Source-directory repository placement
values.description: Place the client repository in a source directory while keeping build artifacts outside its working tree.

values.label: Nested source working directory
values.description: The working tree resides in a nested source directory, leaving sibling locations available.

values.label: Sibling build-output directories
values.description: Build outputs are placed beside rather than inside the Git working directory.

clusters.name: Working-Directory Change Detection
clusters.description: Captures how clients detect filesystem changes efficiently, distinguishing Git-aware monitoring from general-purpose filesystem watching.

relations.reading: Choices on Working-Directory Change Detection affect the outcomes of Client Index Representation
relations.rationale: The amount and selectivity of detected filesystem work influence how often the index is inspected and rewritten.

values.label: Custom Git-aware filesystem watcher
values.description: Git-integrated watching understands ignore rules and avoids scanning directories that cannot contain relevant changes.

values.label: Watchman filesystem watcher
values.description: A general-purpose watcher lacks the Git-specific behavior and efficiency required by Scalar.

values.label: Reduced large-checkout status latency
values.description: Git status becomes substantially faster when monitoring narrows inspection to modified paths.

clusters.name: Client Index Representation
clusters.description: Which client-side index representation and caching approach supports scalable tracked-path lookup and status operations?

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: The index records every tracked path at the current HEAD.

values.label: Updated compact index format
values.description: A newer index representation reduces storage required for millions of entries.

values.label: Untracked-file cache
values.description: Cached untracked-file information reduces repeated work in repositories containing very many files.

values.label: Single-file index stream I/O
values.description: Core commands read and write the index as one streamed file.

values.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
values.description: The updated index format reduces a very large repository index from approximately 400 MB to 250 MB.

values.label: Low index-entry processing time
values.description: Streaming one index file keeps average processing time per entry low despite the index size.

clusters.name: Git Object Storage Representation
clusters.description: Which representation stores Git objects for scalable lookup, maintenance, and repository hosting?

values.label: Multi-pack index representation
values.description: An index maps objects across multiple accumulated packfiles without rewriting all repository data into one pack.

values.label: Pack-based object storage
values.description: Git objects are stored in delta-compressed packfiles rather than as individual loose-object files.

values.label: Server-side non-packfile representation
values.description: Hosting internals may use representations other than client-facing packfiles while preserving Git network interoperability.

values.label: Distributed key-value Git-object storage
values.description: Store content-addressed Git objects in a distributed key-value system instead of conventional packfiles.

values.label: JGit repository-storage abstraction
values.description: Use a custom Git implementation abstraction to replace ordinary on-disk packfiles with another object store.

values.label: Filesystem-resident packfile authority
values.description: Repository state is maintained in filesystem-resident packfiles on hosting machines.

values.label: Blob-storage Git packfiles
values.description: Store large Git packfiles in scalable blob storage rather than requiring them on replica disks.

values.label: Standard on-disk Git repository operations
values.description: Keep Git operations on a normal on-disk repository using established Git tooling.

values.label: Simple storage system
values.description: The storage architecture prioritizes operational simplicity as an overarching repository-storage design direction.

values.label: Full repository repacking cost
values.description: Rewriting all repository data into one pack becomes inefficient as repository size grows.

values.label: Loose-object storage overhead
values.description: Accumulated loose objects consume extra disk space and degrade performance relative to packed storage.

values.label: Pack-index accumulation lookup cost
values.description: Object lookup slows as the number of pack indexes grows without multi-pack indexing.

clusters.name: Git Object Traversal and Transfer
clusters.description: Which traversal and network-transfer mechanism provides scalable access to Git history and objects?

values.label: Sequential Git DAG traversal
values.description: Traverse commit, tree, parent, and file pointers sequentially to locate dependent Git objects.

values.label: Packfile Git network transfer
values.description: Transfer Git data over the network as packfiles regardless of server-side object storage.

values.label: Commit-and-tree-only initial clone
values.description: Initial cloning transfers commits and trees while omitting other Git objects.

values.label: On-demand Git object retrieval
values.description: Missing Git objects are fetched only when client operations require them.

values.label: Distributed-store DAG round-trip cost
values.description: Incur a network round trip for each sequential distributed-store object lookup during Git DAG traversal.

values.label: Unacceptable distributed-object clone performance
values.description: Experience clone performance poor enough to discard distributed object storage.

values.label: Complete-object clone and verification burden
values.description: Complete cloning requires transferring and verifying all repository objects, creating substantial cost.

clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
clusters.description: Is repository hosting organized centrally or through a distributed repository model?

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: A central host stores and serves repositories for users and organizations.

values.label: Distributed repository model
values.description: Repositories remain distributed across developers or maintainers rather than relying solely on a central host.

values.label: Offline distributed workflow
values.description: The distributed model permits offline work and delayed pushes even when users also rely on centralized hosting.

values.label: Centralized-workflow mismatch
values.description: Git's distributed model can hinder workflows organized around a centralized host.

values.label: Large-scale hosting difficulty
values.description: Operating Git repository hosting at large scale creates substantial engineering and operational complexity.

clusters.name: Client Remote Synchronization
clusters.description: How are remote objects, references, and commit metadata synchronized between clients and hosted repositories?

values.label: Background object prefetch with foreground reference updates
values.description: Clients prefetch objects in the background while users explicitly control when remote-reference updates become visible.

values.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
values.description: Fetched remote references are stored separately from normal remote-tracking refs to support metadata generation without changing user-visible refs.

values.label: Background split commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Clients update reachable-commit graph metadata incrementally in background work rather than coupling it to foreground fetches.

values.label: Fetch-time commit-graph writing
values.description: Writing the commit-graph synchronously during fetch adds foreground work.

values.label: Foreground fetch commit-graph overhead
values.description: Writing commit-graph data during foreground fetches adds user-visible fetch overhead.

clusters.name: Compaction Coordination
clusters.description: Which repository replica performs compaction and how are its results propagated to other replicas?

values.label: Primary-only compaction
values.description: Only the primary replica performs compaction, avoiding concurrent CPU-intensive maintenance on replicas.

values.label: Replica-side repacking
values.description: Each replica independently performs repacking as part of repository maintenance.

values.label: WAL-recorded compaction propagation
values.description: Compaction results are recorded in the write-ahead log so replicas reproduce the result through normal log following.

values.label: Pre-compacted pack distribution
values.description: Replicas receive already-compacted packfiles from shared object storage instead of consuming replica CPU to repack.

values.label: Unbounded WAL growth
values.description: Without periodic compaction, restoration must replay an increasingly long write-ahead log.

values.label: Replica repacking availability burden
values.description: Independent repacking across replicas consumes CPU and can overlap maintenance, creating availability and failover risk.

clusters.name: Repository State Authority
clusters.description: Where is authoritative repository state maintained, on replica disks or in an external durable log?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository State Authority limit the options available on Repository Placement and Routing
relations.rationale: The WAL-authoritative design permits stateless placement and rematerialization, while on-disk authority requires tracked replica locations.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead-log authority
values.description: Authoritative repository state resides in an external S3 write-ahead log, allowing disposable repository instances.

values.label: On-disk replica authority
values.description: Repository copies on local disks are authoritative for consensus and correctness.

values.label: Local-disk warm-cache copies
values.description: Local repository copies accelerate access but remain non-authoritative caches.

values.label: Packfile-induced scale limitation
values.description: Filesystem-backed packfiles limit repository availability and scalability at large hosting scale.

clusters.name: Repository Placement and Routing
clusters.description: How are repository instances assigned, located, and rematerialized across hosting nodes?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Placement and Routing affect the outcomes of Reference Update Ordering
relations.rationale: Replica distance and placement directly affect reference-update latency, throughput, and availability.

values.label: Stateless repository placement
values.description: Repositories may reside on any healthy node without persistent authoritative placement state.

values.label: External repository-routing database
values.description: A centralized database maps each repository to every machine hosting its replicas.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashing routing
values.description: Repository IDs are mapped to expected healthy nodes using rendezvous hashing without authoritative routing tables.

values.label: WAL-based repository rematerialization
values.description: Missing or misplaced local copies are recreated on an available node from durable WAL state.

values.label: Single-machine repository storage
values.description: Each repository is hosted on one server behind a conventional filesystem-backed service.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica sizing
values.description: Replica counts vary with repository demand, from one replica to hundreds.

values.label: Dedicated fileserver repository placement
values.description: Repositories reside on dedicated fileservers while applications access them remotely.

values.label: Pet-style repository management
values.description: Each repository is individually located, monitored, validated, and repaired rather than treated as interchangeable.

values.label: Multi-disk multi-machine repository placement
values.description: A repository is distributed across multiple disks and machines for parallel operation and crash availability.

values.label: Single-machine repository placement
values.description: Each repository resides on one machine, leaving availability and hot-repository performance exposed.

values.label: Horizontal scalability from remote repository operations
values.description: Remote repository operations allow application-side horizontal scaling without filesystem replication.

values.label: Repository-location metadata dependency
values.description: External placement metadata becomes an availability dependency for locating replicated repositories.

clusters.name: Reference Update Ordering
clusters.description: How are concurrent reference updates ordered, validated, serialized, and recovered across replicas?

values.label: Per-write majority voting
values.description: Every reference update is ordered and becomes durable through a majority vote across replicas.

values.label: Single-primary write ordering
values.description: A designated primary dictates the order that replicas apply all writes.

values.label: Atomic compare-and-swap WAL updates
values.description: Any repository instance can accept concurrent pushes through atomic compare-and-swap updates to the WAL.

values.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
values.description: Writes that fail majority agreement are reverted on every replica where they were applied.

values.label: Unhealthy marking of dissenting replicas
values.description: Replicas that lose a write vote leave service until repaired.

values.label: Replica-independent push acceptance
values.description: Any server may accept a push without consensus-based primary assignment when WAL updates are atomically protected.

values.label: Consensus elections for repository primaries
values.description: A consensus protocol elects a primary server responsible for accepting repository writes.

values.label: Majority-locked write serialization
values.description: Acquire an exclusive majority lock so conflicting reference writes cannot proceed concurrently.

values.label: Linearized push processing
values.description: Process all pushes in one ordered history to prevent races between concurrent updates.

values.label: Single-local-repository reference synchronization
values.description: Reference transactions synchronize through one local repository rather than a replica quorum.

values.label: Concurrent-write elimination
values.description: Eliminate repository conflicts caused by concurrent reference updates through serialized majority locking.

clusters.name: Write Commitment and Durability
clusters.description: How many replicas and which commit protocol make a repository write durable or refuse unsafe writes?

values.label: Unsafe-replication write refusal
values.description: Refuse writes that cannot be committed to the required replicas safely.

values.label: Unconditional write acceptance
values.description: Accept writes regardless of whether the required replication guarantee can be maintained.

values.label: Three-phase replica commit
values.description: Coordinate updates to distant replicas with a three-phase commit protocol.

values.label: WAL durability before push acknowledgment
values.description: Acknowledge a push only after the complete operation is durably persisted in the write-ahead log.

values.label: Three-replica voting configuration
values.description: Each repository uses three replicas to provide redundancy and continued pushes when one machine fails.

values.label: Two-copy synchronous commitment
values.description: Require synchronous commitment to two replicas before accepting a write.

values.label: Minimum replica-count write threshold
values.description: Use the ability to create the required minimum number of copies as the write-acceptance condition.

values.label: Two-copy durability strategy
values.description: Use one additional copy as the durability strategy rather than a larger quorum or conflict-serialization scheme.

values.label: Durability-induced write unavailability
values.description: Temporarily lose write availability when the replication guarantee cannot be maintained.

values.label: Consensus tail-latency amplification
values.description: Adding coordinated replicas increases transaction latency because each phase waits for the slowest server.

values.label: Replica-count push-throughput degradation
values.description: Increasing coordinated replica count reduces push throughput because every server participates in commit.

values.label: Idle-replica resource overhead
values.description: Maintaining multiple replicas for many small repositories consumes resources even when replicas are mostly idle.

clusters.name: Reference Update Performance
clusters.description: Which throughput, latency, overlap, and read-preservation strategy governs reference-update performance?

values.label: Few-hundred-millisecond update budget
values.description: The required per-update throughput implies a few-hundred-millisecond latency budget.

values.label: Transient disagreement without availability impact
values.description: Occasional non-unanimous votes do not normally reduce repository availability because service continues from the majority.

values.label: Replication-latency throughput limitation
values.description: Greater replica distance increases update latency and lowers sustainable per-repository reference-update throughput.

values.label: Read-preserving write optimization
values.description: Reference-update optimizations must preserve read performance because reads greatly outnumber writes.

values.label: Overlapped network-wait work
values.description: Perform independent locking, checksum, and database activities in parallel while replica network operations wait.

values.label: Per-repository update throughput target
values.description: Replication coordination is sized to sustain several reference updates per second for one repository.

values.label: Batched WAL ingestion
values.description: Batching WAL writes amortizes object-storage request latency and raises push throughput.

values.label: One-object-storage-write-per-push ingestion
values.description: Issuing one object-storage write for every push imposes a throughput ceiling.

clusters.name: Replica Failure Detection
clusters.description: Which application-level signals and routing policies detect failed repository replicas and limit false failover?

values.label: Live-operation failure detection
values.description: Detect replica failure from repeated failed Git or RPC operations and route requests away without waiting for a separate detector.

values.label: Combined heartbeat and traffic detection
values.description: Combine heartbeat liveness checks with real application traffic to detect failures and confirm recovery.

values.label: Heartbeat-only failure detection
values.description: Use heartbeats alone as the primary health signal for repository replicas.

values.label: Application-server-local failure views
values.description: Maintain replica failure state independently at each application server rather than relying on one global view.

values.label: Consecutive-failure offline threshold
values.description: Mark a replica offline only after a configured sequence of failed requests, reducing reactions to isolated errors.

values.label: Preference-ordered replica failover
values.description: Try replicas in a preference order and demote repeatedly failing nodes without permanently excluding them.

values.label: No-op-only health checks
values.description: Use no-op checks alone to determine whether a repository replica is healthy for authenticated Git operations.

values.label: Cross-server failure correlation
values.description: Correlate independent application-server failure reports to distinguish a bad file server from a faulty reporting application server.

values.label: Heartbeat-based node recovery signal
values.description: Heartbeats can signal that a previously unavailable repository node has recovered.

values.label: Advisory replica demotion
values.description: A replica may be demoted from preferred service without being treated as permanently failed.

values.label: RPC failover health telemetry
values.description: Failover behavior supplies server-health telemetry used in replica failure assessment.

values.label: False-positive replica eviction
values.description: Temporarily remove or demote a healthy replica because random operation failures trigger the failure threshold.

clusters.name: Client Feature Default Policy
clusters.description: Which client features run by default in foreground, background, or disabled modes?

relations.reading: Choices on Client Feature Default Policy affect the outcomes of Working-Directory Change Detection
relations.rationale: Disabling or backgrounding client status features changes interactive filesystem-change detection behavior and latency.

values.label: Compatibility-oriented disabling of foreground features
values.description: Advanced foreground Git work is disabled by default to preserve compatibility and avoid blocking interactive commands.

values.label: Background execution of client maintenance
values.description: Client maintenance and metadata generation run asynchronously rather than during interactive operations.

clusters.name: WAL Object-Storage Tier
clusters.description: Which object-storage performance tier supports the write-ahead log's durability and ingestion rate?

relations.reading: Choices on WAL Object-Storage Tier affect the outcomes of Reference Update Performance
relations.rationale: The documents tie object-storage PUT latency and tier selection directly to WAL ingestion and push throughput.

values.label: S3 Standard WAL storage tier
values.description: Standard object storage provides durable WAL storage for moderate push ingestion rates.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone WAL storage tier
values.description: A lower-latency object-storage tier supports higher WAL ingestion rates.

parts.description: Where are repository replicas deployed relative to geography and network proximity?

saturation_history.rationale: Not tested: the taxonomy was generated from this minibatch.

uncovered_concepts: Compaction events recorded in the write-ahead log
Replica capability checks for reference updates
Preservation of local and remote-tracking branches
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers the broad replication mechanism, consistency guarantee, placement, maintenance scheduling, sparse working-tree, filesystem watching, and client index dimensions. However, several relevant architectural axes are missing. First, server-side object-database compaction is not captured: the taxonomy has general maintenance execution, but not the distinct choice of who performs repacking, how compaction is propagated through the WAL, whether replicas consume pre-compacted packs, or how multi-pack indexes and incremental geometric compaction avoid full repacks. Second, replica coordination is under-specified: consistency freshness does not capture three-phase commit, atomic multi-reference transactions, capability checks, deterministic commit/rollback, or the associated replication-factor and quorum trade-offs. Third, the client strategy of separating background object prefetch from foreground reference updates—using hidden refs while preserving normal local and remote-tracking branches—is not represented by the existing maintenance dimension. Finally, the taxonomy lacks a deployment/hosting-topology axis covering the transition from a single-machine centralized host to replicated centralized hosting. The filesystem, packfile, and Git-level distribution alternatives themselves are covered by the existing Replication Integration Layer, but the hosting topology and the missing coordination and compaction decisions are not.

uncovered_concepts: S3 write-ahead log as repository source of truth
WAL-based repository rematerialization after placement mismatch
On-disk repositories as consensus source of truth
saturation_history.rationale: The minibatch is not theoretically saturated. Existing dimensions cover packfile storage and incremental repacking, client maintenance and fsmonitor, replica geography, replication mechanisms such as DRBD and Spokes, and several quorum/read-routing consequences. However, the open codes also introduce distinct architectural axes that the taxonomy does not capture: authoritative repository state versus local warm caches; stateless rematerialization versus persistent placement; routing derived from rendezvous hashing versus maintained in an external repository-location database; server-side repository representation beyond filesystem-resident packfiles; and distributing one repository across multiple disks or machines rather than merely placing replicas geographically. The Spokes material further exposes a missing write-coordination and replica-health dimension: per-write voting versus single-primary ordering, CAS-based concurrent updates, rollback of losing writes, unhealthy-replica exclusion, automated repair, and quorum preservation under corruption or server loss. These concepts matter directly to large-scale hosting reliability and operational scalability and cannot be absorbed by the existing freshness, replica-placement, read-routing, or maintenance dimensions without conflating different decision axes.

uncovered_concepts: Write refusal when replication is unsafe
saturation_history.rationale: The minibatch is largely covered. Index compression, background fetch and commit-graph/MIDX maintenance, filesystem monitoring, partial clone, sparse checkout, replication factor, majority acknowledgment, write serialization, checksumming, WAL durability, linearized pushes, replica rewind, and distributed object-storage alternatives can be absorbed by the existing indexing, maintenance, replication, consistency, coordination, and repository-authority dimensions. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct axis for localized failure detection and the containment of failure-detector false positives; maintenance safety describes how failures are handled, not how availability is independently assessed. It also lacks an explicit degraded-write admission policy that weighs durability and partition tolerance against write availability, including the threshold for accepting writes and refusing unsafe writes. Finally, it has no dimension for Git client feature-integration and distribution strategy, such as shipping a custom Git distribution versus contributing features upstream to core Git. These are relevant architectural decisions for large-scale hosting and clients and cannot be added without conflating different axes.

uncovered_concepts: Combined heartbeat and real-traffic failure detection
Compatibility-oriented default disabling of advanced features
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes: replication factor and quorum are represented by Replica Read Routing and Reference-Update Coordination; placement across racks or regions fits Replica Placement; repair, quiescing, rolling maintenance, and retirement fit Maintenance Transition Safety; and Scalar, GVFS, partial clone, core Git integration, and background maintenance fit the existing client-side dimensions. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct architectural decision about failure-health detection and failure-state dissemination: whether to use heartbeats, live application traffic, no-op checks, consecutive-failure thresholds, local versus correlated failure views, and advisory versus definitive replica demotion. These choices directly affect request routing and availability but are not merely replica placement, read routing, or maintenance execution. In addition, compatibility-oriented default enablement versus explicit or tool-managed activation of advanced Git performance features is not captured by the existing dimensions; automatic configuration and core-Git integration do not specify that compatibility trade-off.

uncovered_concepts: S3 Express One Zone storage tier
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: background maintenance and commit-graph generation fit Maintenance Execution Mode and Client Remote Synchronization; GVFS, sparse checkout, on-demand retrieval, caching, and working-directory layout fit Working-Tree Population Strategy; WAL authority, durability-before-acknowledgment, publication ordering, replica consistency, fan-out, and 3PC fit the existing authority, consistency, reference-ordering, and commitment dimensions; and filesystem, packfile, and replication alternatives are already represented. However, several relevant architectural axes remain distinct. RPC-based repository access concerns the access/decomposition boundary between application servers and repository fileservers, not merely repository placement. One-write-per-push versus batched WAL writes concerns WAL ingestion and persistence batching, while the S3 Standard versus S3 Express One Zone choices concern the WAL storage-performance tier; neither axis is represented explicitly. Single-local-repository reference synchronization captures whether reference transactions are coordinated through one local repository or across a replica quorum, which is distinct from the existing durability outcome. Elastic per-repository replica sizing captures demand-based replication-factor policy, not just placement or commitment count. Finally, disabling ahead/behind calculation is a client status-computation policy not captured by filesystem change detection, index representation, or remote synchronization.

selected_clusters.name: Replication Mechanism
selected_clusters.description: Which mechanism carries repository updates between replicas, from Git-aware and packfile methods to gossip or asynchronous propagation?

relations.reading: Choices on Replication Mechanism affect the outcomes of Repository Consistency Guarantee
relations.rationale: Replication mechanisms determine whether replicas can remain fully synchronized and what complexity and failure behavior the consistency model entails.

values.label: Git application-level replication
values.description: Replicate repositories through application-level Git operations, optionally combined with rsync for scalable synchronization and repair.

values.label: Packfile-level replication
values.description: Replication operates on Git packfiles while leaving Git itself undistributed.

values.label: Filesystem block-level replication
values.description: Replication copies filesystem blocks as the older architecture.

values.label: Git system distribution
values.description: Git is distributed as a system-level component requiring maintenance of a suitable fork.

values.label: Optimistic UDP gossip replication
values.description: Replicas exchange WAL metadata through lossy UDP gossip and independently validate durable state.

values.label: Asynchronous packfile distribution
values.description: Large pushed packfiles distribute without consensus because unreachable objects need not be synchronized immediately.

values.label: Whole-packfile local caching
values.description: Caching complete packfiles locally can make random access acceptable but does not scale across very many repositories.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Distribution Architecture
selected_clusters.description: How are repository copies exposed, distributed, and fanned out across hosting infrastructure?

values.label: Proxy-mediated replica distribution
values.description: A proxy accepts client pushes and distributes updates to multiple fileservers.

values.label: Filesystem-level repository distribution
values.description: The filesystem containing Git data is distributed while the application remains unchanged.

values.label: Packfile-level repository distribution
values.description: Packfiles rather than the whole filesystem are distributed among repository-serving locations.

values.label: NFS-backed repository distribution
values.description: A network filesystem such as NFS provides distributed storage for centralized repositories.

values.label: RPC-based repository access
values.description: Applications access repositories through RPC while repositories remain on dedicated fileservers.

values.label: Multi-server repository replication
values.description: Each repository has copies on multiple servers for resilience and distributed serving.

values.label: Orchestrated push fan-out
values.description: An orchestrator distributes pushed packfiles to repository replicas.

values.label: Network-filesystem correctness and performance problems
values.description: Networked filesystem semantics can make Git operations slow and buggy because Git assumes local-disk behavior.

values.label: Durable highly available repository access
values.description: Preserve repository access and durability despite server and network failures through replicated storage.

values.label: Central-server stress reduction
values.description: Proxy caching reduces repeated object-serving work handled by the central server.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Consistency Guarantee
selected_clusters.description: Which freshness, consistency, and partition-priority guarantee do repository replicas provide?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Consistency Guarantee limit the options available on Replica Placement
relations.rationale: Read routing must account for replica freshness when replicas are geographically dispersed; stale replicas cannot serve reads requiring current repository state.

values.label: Fully synchronized repository replicas
values.description: All replicas maintain current repository state so clients and CI can immediately observe updates.

values.label: Eventually consistent repository views
values.description: Replicas may temporarily omit newly pushed commits, creating unreliable client and CI behavior.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition priority
values.description: Prioritize consistency and partition tolerance over availability when replication or communication failures occur.

values.label: Immediate post-push commit visibility
values.description: Reliable visibility of newly pushed commits is the operational result of strong synchronization.

values.label: Full-consistency implementation complexity
values.description: Maintaining complete synchronization imposes substantial implementation complexity.

values.label: Globally consistent reads across replicas
values.description: Replication and durable-state validation provide a consistent repository view across replicas.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Consistency Enforcement
selected_clusters.description: Which read-validation or catch-up mechanism enforces the selected repository consistency guarantee?

values.label: ETag-validated replica reads
values.description: Conditional object-store validation checks replica freshness before serving reads.

values.label: Read-time replica catch-up
values.description: A replica catches up from durable storage when validation detects a newer WAL index.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Placement
selected_clusters.description: Where are repository replicas deployed relative to geography and network proximity?

relations.reading: Choices on Replica Placement affect the outcomes of Repository Failure Transition
relations.rationale: Distributing reads across replicas and excluding unavailable hosts enables maintenance without interrupting new reads or losing service capacity.

values.label: Geographically dispersed replica placement
values.description: Replicas span separated datacenters or geographic areas for disaster survivability and closer user access.

values.label: Low-latency replica proximity
values.description: Replicas remain relatively close to the proxy to satisfy communication-latency requirements.

values.label: Co-located fileserver replicas
values.description: Replicas are kept adjacent to one another to satisfy latency-sensitive block replication.

values.label: Rack-separated replica placement
values.description: Place repository replicas in distinct racks treated as availability zones to withstand rack-wide failures.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Read Routing
selected_clusters.description: How are replicas selected for reads and assigned voting or non-voting participation?

values.label: Freshness-aware nearest-replica routing
values.description: Reads use the nearest replica that has been assessed as up to date.

values.label: Non-voting geographic replicas
values.description: Geographic replicas serve reads without being required for push quorum, preserving write availability during reachability failures.

values.label: Single-replica read routing
values.description: Reads route to any one up-to-date replica without cross-replica read coordination.

values.label: Improved geographic transfer speed
values.description: Users near replicas experience faster Git transfers as a result of geographic, freshness-aware read serving.

values.label: Linear read scaling through replication
values.description: Adding replicas increases read throughput approximately linearly without reducing push throughput.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Failure Transition
selected_clusters.description: Which failure and recovery behavior governs repository access when a server crashes or becomes unavailable?

relations.reading: Repository Failure Transition requires Maintenance Execution Mode to be decided first
relations.rationale: Safe server retirement depends on knowing how ongoing maintenance and repository operations are scheduled and executed.

values.label: Crash-recovery maintenance logic
values.description: Planned maintenance reuses recovery mechanisms designed for crashes and permanent failures.

values.label: Immediate server reboot or unplugging
values.description: Abrupt retirement interrupts long-running reads and can discard their progress.

values.label: Interrupted long-running reads
values.description: Direct reboot can force large clones and other reads to restart elsewhere, losing prior progress.

selected_clusters.name: Server Reboot Maintenance Policy
selected_clusters.description: How are servers drained, rebooted, and concurrency-limited during planned maintenance?

values.label: Quiescing before reboot
values.description: The server drains active operations before shutdown and stops accepting new reads.

values.label: Rolling reboot maintenance
values.description: Perform maintenance through sequential server or rack reboots while preserving service availability.

values.label: Random server reboot testing
values.description: Randomly reboot file servers to test failure handling while production reads may be active.

values.label: Bounded reboot concurrency
values.description: Limit the number of servers rebooted concurrently within a maintenance zone to preserve redundancy and service access.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Integrity Verification
selected_clusters.description: Which checksum strategy verifies repository integrity efficiently during operation and recovery?

values.label: Continuous repository checksumming
values.description: Repository copies are continually checksummed to detect corruption and unhealthy on-disk state.

values.label: Incremental repository checksum maintenance
values.description: Maintain replica-state checksums incrementally from prior state and changed references.

values.label: From-scratch repository checksum recomputation
values.description: Recompute a replica checksum from the complete reference list after each update.

values.label: XOR reference-pair checksum aggregation
values.description: Aggregate reference-name/value hashes with XOR so changed references can be removed and replaced incrementally.

values.label: Localized failure-detection false positives
values.description: Confine an incorrect server-level failure conclusion to the detecting application server without disrupting production traffic.

values.label: Rapid corruption-recovery requirement
values.description: Corruption detection and repair must be rapid to preserve push availability when replicas are authoritative.

selected_clusters.name: Write Continuity During Maintenance
selected_clusters.description: How do replication and quorum choices preserve writes during server maintenance?

values.label: Continued write replication during quiescing
values.description: Writes continue reaching the quiescing replica so it does not fall arbitrarily behind.

values.label: Replica-tolerant write quorum
values.description: Remaining replicas can continue an in-progress write when one rebooting replica drops out.

selected_clusters.name: Maintenance Execution Mode
selected_clusters.description: How and when is repository maintenance initiated, run, blocked, or disabled by operators?

relations.reading: Choices on Maintenance Execution Mode affect the outcomes of Working-Tree Population Mode
relations.rationale: Maintenance choices such as background cleanup and fetch scheduling change client-side repository performance and the practicality of large working trees.

values.label: Background maintenance through registration
values.description: Registered repositories receive automatic configuration, fetching, commit-graph, and cleanup operations.

values.label: Foreground operator-controlled maintenance
values.description: Operators invoke maintenance on demand or according to their own schedule.

values.label: Single-command maintenance execution
values.description: One command runs the repository’s configuration, fetching, commit-graph, and cleanup tasks together.

values.label: Periodic foreground garbage collection
values.description: The client periodically performs foreground garbage collection despite the impracticality for very large repositories.

values.label: Command-triggered synchronous garbage collection
values.description: User-facing Git commands synchronously invoke complete automatic object-data rewrites.

values.label: Maintenance opt-out controls
values.description: Allow operators to pause or unregister repositories from background maintenance.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Incremental maintenance reduces thousands of packs and large storage footprints to substantially smaller repositories.

values.label: Foreground command blocking
values.description: Large synchronous maintenance operations delay simple interactive Git commands.

values.label: Maintenance resource exhaustion
values.description: Complete repository rewrites can consume CPU and memory and stall the client system.

values.label: Performance decay without automatic collection
values.description: Disabling automatic collection avoids synchronous cost but allows accumulated objects to degrade Git performance.

values.label: Git command acceleration
values.description: Improve interactive Git command performance as the result of repository registration and maintenance.

selected_clusters.name: Maintenance Compaction Strategy
selected_clusters.description: Which compaction and obsolete-pack expiration strategy manages repository storage during maintenance?

values.label: Incremental geometric compaction
values.description: Maintenance incrementally compacts packfiles geometrically before a full repack is needed.

values.label: Small-pack batch repacking
values.description: Maintenance rewrites bounded batches of small packs instead of rewriting all repository data at once.

values.label: Deferred obsolete-pack expiration
values.description: Obsolete packs remain until no multi-pack-index references remain, allowing concurrent Git commands to continue.

values.label: Two-phase repack and expiration
values.description: Replacement-pack creation and indexing are separated from deletion of unreferenced packs.

selected_clusters.name: Maintenance Scheduling Policy
selected_clusters.description: How are bookkeeping and user updates prioritized, coalesced, and delayed during maintenance?

values.label: Bookkeeping-update coalescing
values.description: Cascading bookkeeping reference changes are combined into fewer transactions.

values.label: User-update priority scheduling
values.description: User-initiated reference updates receive priority over non-time-critical bookkeeping work.

values.label: Bookkeeping-update processing delay
values.description: Large bookkeeping cascades can keep repositories busy and delay or time out user updates.

selected_clusters.name: Working-Tree Population Mode
selected_clusters.description: Which population model controls the files and objects materialized in a client working tree?

relations.reading: Choices on Working-Tree Population Mode limit the options available on Working-Directory Change Detection
relations.rationale: The populated-tree strategy determines which paths need monitoring and whether a watcher can avoid scanning irrelevant directories.

values.label: Sparse-checkout population
values.description: Only selected repository paths are populated, scaling working-tree size through Git-native mechanisms.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem population
values.description: A virtual filesystem defers populated-size costs and presents repository content through virtualization.

values.label: Partial-clone GVFS integration
values.description: GVFS interaction is implemented through Git’s partial-clone interface so both mechanisms reinforce one another.

values.label: Full working-directory population
values.description: The client materializes the complete working directory instead of using sparse population.

values.label: Checkout performance bottleneck
values.description: Moving from virtualization to sparse-checkout makes checkout slower than with the former virtual filesystem.

values.label: Populated-file modification detection cost
values.description: Detecting modifications across populated files becomes expensive as the working set grows.

values.label: Higher file-population cost than index adjustment
values.description: Materializing files requires substantially more data handling than adjusting index entries.

values.label: Reduced Git working-tree management burden
values.description: Selective population and separated outputs reduce the work required to manage the working tree.

selected_clusters.name: Client Repository Integration
selected_clusters.description: Which client and protocol integration supplies large-repository capabilities through Git, GVFS, or custom distribution?

values.label: Co-located GVFS cache server
values.description: A cache server near sufficiently large repositories supports GVFS requests for large user groups.

values.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
values.description: GVFS deployment proceeds without the cache-server infrastructure required for scalable operation.

values.label: Git protocol with Scalar registration
values.description: Existing Git-protocol repositories use Scalar registration when GVFS cache infrastructure cannot be resourced.

values.label: Custom Git client distribution
values.description: Distribute a custom Git client containing repository-scaling features.

values.label: Core Git feature integration
values.description: Contribute scaling features to core Git to remove the custom-client requirement.

values.label: GVFS protocol in standard Git client
values.description: Expose the GVFS protocol as the standard Git client's large-repository transfer mechanism.

selected_clusters.name: Repository and Build Placement
selected_clusters.description: How are the repository, source tree, and build outputs arranged on the client filesystem?

values.label: Source-directory repository placement
values.description: Place the client repository in a source directory while keeping build artifacts outside its working tree.

values.label: Nested source working directory
values.description: The working tree resides in a nested source directory, leaving sibling locations available.

values.label: Sibling build-output directories
values.description: Build outputs are placed beside rather than inside the Git working directory.

selected_clusters.name: Working-Directory Change Detection
selected_clusters.description: Captures how clients detect filesystem changes efficiently, distinguishing Git-aware monitoring from general-purpose filesystem watching.

relations.reading: Choices on Working-Directory Change Detection affect the outcomes of Client Index Representation
relations.rationale: The amount and selectivity of detected filesystem work influence how often the index is inspected and rewritten.

values.label: Custom Git-aware filesystem watcher
values.description: Git-integrated watching understands ignore rules and avoids scanning directories that cannot contain relevant changes.

values.label: Watchman filesystem watcher
values.description: A general-purpose watcher lacks the Git-specific behavior and efficiency required by Scalar.

values.label: Reduced large-checkout status latency
values.description: Git status becomes substantially faster when monitoring narrows inspection to modified paths.

selected_clusters.name: Client Index Representation
selected_clusters.description: Which client-side index representation and caching approach supports scalable tracked-path lookup and status operations?

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: The index records every tracked path at the current HEAD.

values.label: Updated compact index format
values.description: A newer index representation reduces storage required for millions of entries.

values.label: Untracked-file cache
values.description: Cached untracked-file information reduces repeated work in repositories containing very many files.

values.label: Single-file index stream I/O
values.description: Core commands read and write the index as one streamed file.

values.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
values.description: The updated index format reduces a very large repository index from approximately 400 MB to 250 MB.

values.label: Low index-entry processing time
values.description: Streaming one index file keeps average processing time per entry low despite the index size.

selected_clusters.name: Git Object Storage Representation
selected_clusters.description: Which representation stores Git objects for scalable lookup, maintenance, and repository hosting?

values.label: Multi-pack index representation
values.description: An index maps objects across multiple accumulated packfiles without rewriting all repository data into one pack.

values.label: Pack-based object storage
values.description: Git objects are stored in delta-compressed packfiles rather than as individual loose-object files.

values.label: Server-side non-packfile representation
values.description: Hosting internals may use representations other than client-facing packfiles while preserving Git network interoperability.

values.label: Distributed key-value Git-object storage
values.description: Store content-addressed Git objects in a distributed key-value system instead of conventional packfiles.

values.label: JGit repository-storage abstraction
values.description: Use a custom Git implementation abstraction to replace ordinary on-disk packfiles with another object store.

values.label: Filesystem-resident packfile authority
values.description: Repository state is maintained in filesystem-resident packfiles on hosting machines.

values.label: Blob-storage Git packfiles
values.description: Store large Git packfiles in scalable blob storage rather than requiring them on replica disks.

values.label: Standard on-disk Git repository operations
values.description: Keep Git operations on a normal on-disk repository using established Git tooling.

values.label: Simple storage system
values.description: The storage architecture prioritizes operational simplicity as an overarching repository-storage design direction.

values.label: Full repository repacking cost
values.description: Rewriting all repository data into one pack becomes inefficient as repository size grows.

values.label: Loose-object storage overhead
values.description: Accumulated loose objects consume extra disk space and degrade performance relative to packed storage.

values.label: Pack-index accumulation lookup cost
values.description: Object lookup slows as the number of pack indexes grows without multi-pack indexing.

selected_clusters.name: Git Object Traversal and Transfer
selected_clusters.description: Which traversal and network-transfer mechanism provides scalable access to Git history and objects?

values.label: Sequential Git DAG traversal
values.description: Traverse commit, tree, parent, and file pointers sequentially to locate dependent Git objects.

values.label: Packfile Git network transfer
values.description: Transfer Git data over the network as packfiles regardless of server-side object storage.

values.label: Commit-and-tree-only initial clone
values.description: Initial cloning transfers commits and trees while omitting other Git objects.

values.label: On-demand Git object retrieval
values.description: Missing Git objects are fetched only when client operations require them.

values.label: Distributed-store DAG round-trip cost
values.description: Incur a network round trip for each sequential distributed-store object lookup during Git DAG traversal.

values.label: Unacceptable distributed-object clone performance
values.description: Experience clone performance poor enough to discard distributed object storage.

values.label: Complete-object clone and verification burden
values.description: Complete cloning requires transferring and verifying all repository objects, creating substantial cost.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
selected_clusters.description: Is repository hosting organized centrally or through a distributed repository model?

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: A central host stores and serves repositories for users and organizations.

values.label: Distributed repository model
values.description: Repositories remain distributed across developers or maintainers rather than relying solely on a central host.

values.label: Offline distributed workflow
values.description: The distributed model permits offline work and delayed pushes even when users also rely on centralized hosting.

values.label: Centralized-workflow mismatch
values.description: Git's distributed model can hinder workflows organized around a centralized host.

values.label: Large-scale hosting difficulty
values.description: Operating Git repository hosting at large scale creates substantial engineering and operational complexity.

selected_clusters.name: Client Remote Synchronization
selected_clusters.description: How are remote objects, references, and commit metadata synchronized between clients and hosted repositories?

values.label: Background object prefetch with foreground reference updates
values.description: Clients prefetch objects in the background while users explicitly control when remote-reference updates become visible.

values.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
values.description: Fetched remote references are stored separately from normal remote-tracking refs to support metadata generation without changing user-visible refs.

values.label: Background split commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Clients update reachable-commit graph metadata incrementally in background work rather than coupling it to foreground fetches.

values.label: Fetch-time commit-graph writing
values.description: Writing the commit-graph synchronously during fetch adds foreground work.

values.label: Foreground fetch commit-graph overhead
values.description: Writing commit-graph data during foreground fetches adds user-visible fetch overhead.

selected_clusters.name: Compaction Coordination
selected_clusters.description: Which repository replica performs compaction and how are its results propagated to other replicas?

values.label: Primary-only compaction
values.description: Only the primary replica performs compaction, avoiding concurrent CPU-intensive maintenance on replicas.

values.label: Replica-side repacking
values.description: Each replica independently performs repacking as part of repository maintenance.

values.label: WAL-recorded compaction propagation
values.description: Compaction results are recorded in the write-ahead log so replicas reproduce the result through normal log following.

values.label: Pre-compacted pack distribution
values.description: Replicas receive already-compacted packfiles from shared object storage instead of consuming replica CPU to repack.

values.label: Unbounded WAL growth
values.description: Without periodic compaction, restoration must replay an increasingly long write-ahead log.

values.label: Replica repacking availability burden
values.description: Independent repacking across replicas consumes CPU and can overlap maintenance, creating availability and failover risk.

selected_clusters.name: Repository State Authority
selected_clusters.description: Where is authoritative repository state maintained, on replica disks or in an external durable log?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository State Authority limit the options available on Repository Placement and Routing
relations.rationale: The WAL-authoritative design permits stateless placement and rematerialization, while on-disk authority requires tracked replica locations.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead-log authority
values.description: Authoritative repository state resides in an external S3 write-ahead log, allowing disposable repository instances.

values.label: On-disk replica authority
values.description: Repository copies on local disks are authoritative for consensus and correctness.

values.label: Local-disk warm-cache copies
values.description: Local repository copies accelerate access but remain non-authoritative caches.

values.label: Packfile-induced scale limitation
values.description: Filesystem-backed packfiles limit repository availability and scalability at large hosting scale.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Placement and Routing
selected_clusters.description: How are repository instances assigned, located, and rematerialized across hosting nodes?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Placement and Routing affect the outcomes of Reference Update Ordering
relations.rationale: Replica distance and placement directly affect reference-update latency, throughput, and availability.

values.label: Stateless repository placement
values.description: Repositories may reside on any healthy node without persistent authoritative placement state.

values.label: External repository-routing database
values.description: A centralized database maps each repository to every machine hosting its replicas.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashing routing
values.description: Repository IDs are mapped to expected healthy nodes using rendezvous hashing without authoritative routing tables.

values.label: WAL-based repository rematerialization
values.description: Missing or misplaced local copies are recreated on an available node from durable WAL state.

values.label: Single-machine repository storage
values.description: Each repository is hosted on one server behind a conventional filesystem-backed service.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica sizing
values.description: Replica counts vary with repository demand, from one replica to hundreds.

values.label: Dedicated fileserver repository placement
