values.description: Repositories reside on dedicated fileservers while applications access them remotely.

values.label: Pet-style repository management
values.description: Each repository is individually located, monitored, validated, and repaired rather than treated as interchangeable.

values.label: Multi-disk multi-machine repository placement
values.description: A repository is distributed across multiple disks and machines for parallel operation and crash availability.

values.label: Single-machine repository placement
values.description: Each repository resides on one machine, leaving availability and hot-repository performance exposed.

values.label: Horizontal scalability from remote repository operations
values.description: Remote repository operations allow application-side horizontal scaling without filesystem replication.

values.label: Repository-location metadata dependency
values.description: External placement metadata becomes an availability dependency for locating replicated repositories.

selected_clusters.name: Reference Update Ordering
selected_clusters.description: How are concurrent reference updates ordered, validated, serialized, and recovered across replicas?

values.label: Per-write majority voting
values.description: Every reference update is ordered and becomes durable through a majority vote across replicas.

values.label: Single-primary write ordering
values.description: A designated primary dictates the order that replicas apply all writes.

values.label: Atomic compare-and-swap WAL updates
values.description: Any repository instance can accept concurrent pushes through atomic compare-and-swap updates to the WAL.

values.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
values.description: Writes that fail majority agreement are reverted on every replica where they were applied.

values.label: Unhealthy marking of dissenting replicas
values.description: Replicas that lose a write vote leave service until repaired.

values.label: Replica-independent push acceptance
values.description: Any server may accept a push without consensus-based primary assignment when WAL updates are atomically protected.

values.label: Consensus elections for repository primaries
values.description: A consensus protocol elects a primary server responsible for accepting repository writes.

values.label: Majority-locked write serialization
values.description: Acquire an exclusive majority lock so conflicting reference writes cannot proceed concurrently.

values.label: Linearized push processing
values.description: Process all pushes in one ordered history to prevent races between concurrent updates.

values.label: Single-local-repository reference synchronization
values.description: Reference transactions synchronize through one local repository rather than a replica quorum.

values.label: Concurrent-write elimination
values.description: Eliminate repository conflicts caused by concurrent reference updates through serialized majority locking.

selected_clusters.name: Write Commitment and Durability
selected_clusters.description: How many replicas and which commit protocol make a repository write durable or refuse unsafe writes?

values.label: Unsafe-replication write refusal
values.description: Refuse writes that cannot be committed to the required replicas safely.

values.label: Unconditional write acceptance
values.description: Accept writes regardless of whether the required replication guarantee can be maintained.

values.label: Three-phase replica commit
values.description: Coordinate updates to distant replicas with a three-phase commit protocol.

values.label: WAL durability before push acknowledgment
values.description: Acknowledge a push only after the complete operation is durably persisted in the write-ahead log.

values.label: Three-replica voting configuration
values.description: Each repository uses three replicas to provide redundancy and continued pushes when one machine fails.

values.label: Two-copy synchronous commitment
values.description: Require synchronous commitment to two replicas before accepting a write.

values.label: Minimum replica-count write threshold
values.description: Use the ability to create the required minimum number of copies as the write-acceptance condition.

values.label: Two-copy durability strategy
values.description: Use one additional copy as the durability strategy rather than a larger quorum or conflict-serialization scheme.

values.label: Durability-induced write unavailability
values.description: Temporarily lose write availability when the replication guarantee cannot be maintained.

values.label: Consensus tail-latency amplification
values.description: Adding coordinated replicas increases transaction latency because each phase waits for the slowest server.

values.label: Replica-count push-throughput degradation
values.description: Increasing coordinated replica count reduces push throughput because every server participates in commit.

values.label: Idle-replica resource overhead
values.description: Maintaining multiple replicas for many small repositories consumes resources even when replicas are mostly idle.

selected_clusters.name: Reference Update Performance
selected_clusters.description: Which throughput, latency, overlap, and read-preservation strategy governs reference-update performance?

values.label: Few-hundred-millisecond update budget
values.description: The required per-update throughput implies a few-hundred-millisecond latency budget.

values.label: Transient disagreement without availability impact
values.description: Occasional non-unanimous votes do not normally reduce repository availability because service continues from the majority.

values.label: Replication-latency throughput limitation
values.description: Greater replica distance increases update latency and lowers sustainable per-repository reference-update throughput.

values.label: Read-preserving write optimization
values.description: Reference-update optimizations must preserve read performance because reads greatly outnumber writes.

values.label: Overlapped network-wait work
values.description: Perform independent locking, checksum, and database activities in parallel while replica network operations wait.

values.label: Per-repository update throughput target
values.description: Replication coordination is sized to sustain several reference updates per second for one repository.

values.label: Batched WAL ingestion
values.description: Batching WAL writes amortizes object-storage request latency and raises push throughput.

values.label: One-object-storage-write-per-push ingestion
values.description: Issuing one object-storage write for every push imposes a throughput ceiling.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Failure Detection
selected_clusters.description: Which application-level signals and routing policies detect failed repository replicas and limit false failover?

values.label: Live-operation failure detection
values.description: Detect replica failure from repeated failed Git or RPC operations and route requests away without waiting for a separate detector.

values.label: Combined heartbeat and traffic detection
values.description: Combine heartbeat liveness checks with real application traffic to detect failures and confirm recovery.

values.label: Heartbeat-only failure detection
values.description: Use heartbeats alone as the primary health signal for repository replicas.

values.label: Application-server-local failure views
values.description: Maintain replica failure state independently at each application server rather than relying on one global view.

values.label: Consecutive-failure offline threshold
values.description: Mark a replica offline only after a configured sequence of failed requests, reducing reactions to isolated errors.

values.label: Preference-ordered replica failover
values.description: Try replicas in a preference order and demote repeatedly failing nodes without permanently excluding them.

values.label: No-op-only health checks
values.description: Use no-op checks alone to determine whether a repository replica is healthy for authenticated Git operations.

values.label: Cross-server failure correlation
values.description: Correlate independent application-server failure reports to distinguish a bad file server from a faulty reporting application server.

values.label: Heartbeat-based node recovery signal
values.description: Heartbeats can signal that a previously unavailable repository node has recovered.

values.label: Advisory replica demotion
values.description: A replica may be demoted from preferred service without being treated as permanently failed.

values.label: RPC failover health telemetry
values.description: Failover behavior supplies server-health telemetry used in replica failure assessment.

values.label: False-positive replica eviction
values.description: Temporarily remove or demote a healthy replica because random operation failures trigger the failure threshold.

selected_clusters.name: Client Feature Default Policy
selected_clusters.description: Which client features run by default in foreground, background, or disabled modes?

relations.reading: Choices on Client Feature Default Policy affect the outcomes of Working-Directory Change Detection
relations.rationale: Disabling or backgrounding client status features changes interactive filesystem-change detection behavior and latency.

values.label: Compatibility-oriented disabling of foreground features
values.description: Advanced foreground Git work is disabled by default to preserve compatibility and avoid blocking interactive commands.

values.label: Background execution of client maintenance
values.description: Client maintenance and metadata generation run asynchronously rather than during interactive operations.

selected_clusters.name: WAL Object-Storage Tier
selected_clusters.description: Which object-storage performance tier supports the write-ahead log's durability and ingestion rate?

relations.reading: Choices on WAL Object-Storage Tier affect the outcomes of Reference Update Performance
relations.rationale: The documents tie object-storage PUT latency and tier selection directly to WAL ingestion and push throughput.

values.label: S3 Standard WAL storage tier
values.description: Standard object storage provides durable WAL storage for moderate push ingestion rates.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone WAL storage tier
values.description: A lower-latency object-storage tier supports higher WAL ingestion rates.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions, such as consistency guarantee (36) versus enforcement mechanism (37), compaction strategy (27) versus compaction coordination (17), and write ordering (28) versus durability (29). However, there are notable overlaps: Replica Placement (9) and Repository Placement and Routing (19) both cover where replicas or repositories reside; refocus 19 on routing/rematerialization and move its physical-placement alternatives to 9 or Repository Distribution Architecture (35). Replication Mechanism (34) and Repository Distribution Architecture (35) also mix update-propagation mechanisms with hosting topology; move propagation choices such as 35.7, Orchestrated push fan-out, to 34 and retain 35 for exposure and distribution structure. Centralized/distributed hosting in Repository Hosting Model (15) partially overlaps the infrastructure distribution choices in 35, so narrow 15 to the repository ownership/workflow model and keep physical distribution in 35.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions are clearly named and their values are usually distinguishable, such as 9 Replica Placement and 31 Replica Failure Detection. However, several dimensions combine different decision questions or levels. Dimension 35 Repository Distribution Architecture mixes proxy access, RPC, replication, fan-out, and outcomes; split or rename it so each question covers one mechanism range. Dimension 36 Repository Consistency Guarantee combines freshness (36.1–36.2) with partition-priority policy (36.3); split these into separate questions. Dimension 22 Git Object Storage Representation mixes pack/index formats, server-side storage, blob storage, and the broad direction 22.9; reorganize these into narrower representation questions and move the outcome values 22.10–22.12 accordingly. Dimension 28 Reference Update Ordering combines majority voting, primary selection, CAS, locking, rollback, and local synchronization; split ordering/serialization alternatives from recovery behavior. Dimension 39 Client Repository Integration combines cache deployment, fallback workflows, custom-client distribution, and core Git integration; separate or rename it to state the specific integration question and keep alternatives at the same level.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: All major decision areas for scaling repositories across servers and clients are represented by dimensions with multiple candidate decisions. Server-side concerns include replication and distribution (34, 35), consistency and durability (36, 28, 29), placement and routing (9, 10, 19), failure handling (31, 41, 42), and maintenance (26, 27). Client and large-repository concerns include object storage and transfer (22, 23), sparse or virtualized working trees (38), synchronization (16), index and filesystem-change detection (7, 21), and client integration (39). Even narrower dimensions such as 37 and 33 contain multiple candidate options, so no major area is left without a multi-option decision point.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions name decisions directly relevant to scaling Git hosting and clients, including replication (34), consistency (36–37), placement and routing (9–10, 19), durability (28–31, 43), maintenance (26–27), and large-client operation (38–39, 7, 21–23). The main scope issues are dimension 15, "Repository Hosting Model," whose generic centralized-versus-distributed workflow decision is broader than scaling the specified hosting systems; dimension 40, "Repository and Build Placement," whose source/build directory layout is only tangential to Git scalability; and dimension 32, "Client Feature Default Policy," whose default-mode policy is less directly an architectural scaling decision. Drop dimensions 15 and 40, and merge dimension 32 into the relevant client maintenance dimension 26 or client integration dimension 39.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: The taxonomy largely avoids catch-all buckets and provides specific decision alternatives or outcomes. Two values in dimension 22, "Git Object Storage Representation," are catch-all-like: 22.3 "Server-side non-packfile representation" uses an open-ended 'other representations' category, and 22.9 "Simple storage system" is explicitly an overarching storage direction. Drop values 22.3 and 22.9, or replace them by reorganizing their specific content into the existing concrete storage dimensions; the remaining values are generally bounded alternatives or identifiable outcomes.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions combine multiple decision points or contain values that are questions of their own. Split 40 (Repository and Build Placement) into separate decisions for repository/source-tree placement and build-output placement, since values 40.1-40.3 are arrangements of different concerns rather than alternatives to one choice. Split 23 (Git Object Traversal and Transfer) into traversal strategy and transfer/clone strategy, since values 23.1-23.4 address distinct mechanisms. Split 17 (Compaction Coordination) into compaction ownership and compaction-result propagation, separating 17.1-17.2 from 17.3-17.4. Reorganize 28 (Reference Update Ordering) into ordering/serialization and failure-recovery decisions, because voting, primary selection, locking, rollback, and unhealthy marking are separate choices. Reorganize 39 (Client Repository Integration) into deployment/infrastructure and client/protocol integration, since 39.1-39.2 concern cache infrastructure while 39.3-39.6 concern Git, GVFS, and custom-client integration.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have at least two candidate values and several are coherent, such as 27 Maintenance Compaction Strategy and 33 WAL Object-Storage Tier. However, many broad dimensions contain values answering different questions. Split 35 Repository Distribution Architecture into separate storage/access and replication/fan-out decisions; its values mix NFS, RPC access, placement, and push distribution. Split 22 Git Object Storage Representation into object representation versus storage location/implementation, and drop or move 22.9 Simple storage system because it is a design goal, not a representation option. Split 28 Reference Update Ordering into ordering/serialization versus commitment and replica-recovery behavior. Split 26 Maintenance Execution Mode into execution scheduling and operator registration/control. Split 39 Client Repository Integration into cache/protocol deployment versus client implementation/distribution. Also move 34.7 Whole-packfile local caching out of Replication Mechanism, since it describes caching rather than carrying updates. These changes preserve at least two candidates per resulting decision and address the main same-question violations.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses and distinguish candidate decisions from effects, but several structural violations remain. In dimension 19, values 19.9 "Multi-disk multi-machine repository placement" and 19.10 "Single-machine repository placement" are phrased as alternative placement decisions, not outcomes; reclassify them as candidate decisions with appropriate statuses. In dimension 32, mixed value 32.1 asserts that foreground features "are disabled by default," which describes a simple adopted policy; revise it to explicitly reflect the conflicting or context-dependent positions. Values 25.6 "Rapid corruption-recovery requirement" and 30.1 "Few-hundred-millisecond update budget" are requirements or targets rather than effects; move them out of the outcome category or drop them.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under existing dimensions. Scalar choices in s04_p01 and s04_p02 map to client integration (39), feature defaults and background maintenance (32, 26), sparse/partial checkout (38), index and filesystem monitoring (21, 7), and repository placement (40). Spokes decisions map to replication and placement (34, 35, 9), consistency and quorum (36, 28, 29), routing and failure handling (10, 31, 41), maintenance (42, 12, 14), and performance (30). Git storage and traversal alternatives in s01_p03, s01_p04, and s01_p05 are covered by 22, 23, and 35. No decision-bearing passage is unplaced, so no taxonomy change is required.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers most adopted and rejected options across the Scalar and Spokes passages, including Git application-level replication (s02_p01), three-phase commit (s02_p03), quorum durability (s03_p02, s03_p09), quiescing and rolling reboots (s03_p07, s03_p08), background maintenance (s05_p09, s05_p11), sparse checkout and partial clone (s04_p02, s05_p04), and WAL/rendezvous-hashing designs (s01_p11). A few specific options are not explicitly named: add 'Git built-in filesystem monitor' to dimension 7, Working-Directory Change Detection, supported by s04_p02; add 'Atomic Git reference-update transactions' to dimension 28, Reference Update Ordering, supported by s02_p04; add 'Cone-mode sparse checkout' to dimension 38, Working-Tree Population Mode, supported by s05_p04; add 'Loose-object cleanup' to dimension 27, Maintenance Compaction Strategy, supported by s05_p12; and add 'Graceful server retirement with replica replenishment' to dimension 42, Server Reboot Maintenance Policy, supported by s03_p09.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: All eight dimensions represent distinct decision questions for scaling Git across servers and clients: replication mechanism (1), consistency guarantee (2), replica placement/routing (3), server maintenance safety (4), repository maintenance execution (5), working-tree population (6), change detection (7), and index representation/access (8). Although dimensions 2 and 3 share freshness concerns and dimensions 1 and 3 both mention replicas, their questions differ: consistency is the visibility guarantee, while replication and routing are mechanisms and deployment choices. No dimension pair asks the same question, so no merge or value relocation is warranted.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy generally makes each decision and its alternative range clear: server-side replication, consistency, placement, maintenance, and client-side working-tree, watcher, and index choices are described with distinguishable labels and explanations. Accepted, rejected, and outcome values are also explicitly identified. The main minor issue is value 8.2, "Updated compact index format": "updated" is vague and does not distinguish the option as precisely as the surrounding values; rename it to "Compact index representation" while retaining its storage-reduction description. Dimension 1, "Replication Integration Layer," could likewise use a more direct decision-oriented name such as "How should repository updates be replicated?".

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the main decision areas implied by scaling Git across many repositories, large repositories, and many users on both servers and clients. Server-side choices have multiple candidates in dimensions 1 (replication mechanisms), 2 (synchronized versus eventually consistent replicas), 3 (placement and routing), and 4 (maintenance strategies); client-side choices are represented in dimensions 5–8 with alternatives for maintenance, working-tree population, change detection, and index handling. Each dimension generally provides several accepted or rejected options, including explicit rejected alternatives such as filesystem replication (1.3), eventual consistency (2.2), immediate rebooting (4.2), virtualized filesystem population (6.2), and Watchman (7.2). No major use-case area lacks a decision point with multiple candidates; only dimension 7 is comparatively narrow, offering two candidates, but that still satisfies the criterion.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: All eight dimensions name architectural decisions within the stated scope of scaling Git across hosting servers and clients. Dimensions 1–5 address server replication, consistency, placement/routing, maintenance safety, and repository maintenance; dimensions 6–8 address client working-tree population, change detection, and index scaling. Their alternatives and outcomes concern very many repositories, very large repositories, and very many users, so no dimension is out of scope or merely tangential under the specified criterion.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No catch-all dimensions or values are present. The eight dimensions use specific decision topics, such as "Replication Integration Layer" and "Working-Directory Change Detection," and their values identify concrete alternatives or outcomes, such as "Filesystem block-level replication," "Watchman filesystem watcher," and "Bookkeeping-update processing delay." No value is labeled or described as Other, Miscellaneous, General considerations, or a similarly broad residual bucket.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains several valid decision areas for scaling repositories across servers and clients, but five dimensions combine distinct decision points rather than presenting one question with alternative answers. Dimension 3, "Replica Placement and Read Routing," mixes placement, read selection, and voting participation; split it into placement (3.1–3.2) and routing/replica participation (3.3–3.4), retaining 3.5 as an outcome. Dimension 4, "Server Maintenance Safety," combines shutdown behavior (4.2–4.3), replication during quiescing (4.4), recovery (4.1), and quorum handling (4.5); reorganize these into separate maintenance-transition and write-continuity decisions. Dimension 5, "Repository Maintenance Execution," combines execution mode (5.1, 5.2, 5.4), command orchestration (5.3), and bookkeeping scheduling (5.5–5.6); split those decisions and keep 5.7 as an outcome. Dimension 6, "Working-Tree Population Strategy," mixes population mechanisms (6.1–6.2), partial-clone/protocol choice (6.3, 6.7), and cache deployment (6.5–6.6); separate these decisions. Dimension 8, "Index Representation and Access," combines index representation (8.1–8.2), untracked-file caching (8.3), and index I/O (8.4); reorganize them so each is a distinct decision, with 8.5–8.6 remaining outcomes. Dimensions 1, 2, and 7 are comparatively closer to the required single-decision structure.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have at least two candidate decisions and several are coherent, including 1 Replication Integration Layer, 2 Repository Consistency Model, 4 Server Maintenance Safety, 7 Working-Directory Change Detection, and 8 Index Representation and Access. The main structural problem is 3 Replica Placement and Read Routing: 3.1–3.2 concern placement, while 3.3–3.4 concern read selection and write participation; split it into those two decision points, each retaining at least two candidates. Dimension 6 Working-Tree Population Strategy also mixes population mechanisms (6.1–6.3) with cache/deployment and fallback choices (6.5–6.7); split those groups into separate decisions. Dimension 5 Repository Maintenance Execution combines execution mode (5.1–5.4) with bookkeeping scheduling and transaction policies (5.5–5.6); separate these questions while retaining the outcome 5.7 with the latter decision. These broad mixed topics reduce alignment despite the taxonomy’s generally strong coverage of scalability, freshness, latency, and availability trade-offs.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: No violations found under the specified taxonomy-status criteria. All values in dimensions 1–8 use an allowed status; rejected options such as 1.3 Filesystem block-level replication, 2.2 Eventually consistent repository views, and 6.2 Virtualized filesystem population are described as declined rather than adopted. Outcome values such as 2.3 Immediate post-push commit visibility, 5.7 Bookkeeping-update processing delay, and 8.5 Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB describe effects rather than alternatives, and no candidate decision is duplicated under conflicting statuses within a dimension.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: Most decision-bearing passages map to the taxonomy: replication choices in s01_p03 and s02_p01, geographic placement in s02_p02, maintenance procedures in s03_p07 and s03_p08, background maintenance in s05_p09 and s05_p11, and sparse/partial checkout in s04_p02 and s05_p04. The main gaps are s01_p11, which discusses rendezvous-hash repository placement and leaderless/arbitrary-primary selection; add values for hash-based routing and primary/leader selection to dimension 3, Replica Placement and Read Routing. s02_p03 discusses choosing three-phase commit and reducing distributed commit round trips; add a commit/consensus protocol dimension or values. s02_p04 discusses Git reference-update transaction semantics and performance optimizations; add values for transactional reference updates and reference-update acceleration, likely under a new replication coordination dimension.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many major options, including application-level versus filesystem replication (s01_p03, s02_p01), geographically dispersed replicas and nearest-fresh reads (s02_p01, s02_p06), quiescing and continued writes during reboot (s03_p07), and background maintenance, sparse checkout, commit graphs, and multi-pack indexes (s04_p02, s05_p09, s05_p11, s05_p12). Key options are still missing: add a value for Git’s builtin File System Monitor to dimension 7, supported by s04_p02; add a value for placing the working directory under `/src` with sibling build-output directories to dimension 6 or a dedicated layout dimension, supported by s04_p02 and s05_p04; add values for three-phase commit, distributed locking, and transactional Git reference updates, supported by s02_p03 and s02_p04; add values for rendezvous-hash routing, S3 write-ahead-log storage, and arbitrary-primary/stateless operation, supported by s01_p11; and add values for rolling rack-by-rack reboots and graceful retirement with replica repair, supported by s03_p08 and s03_p09. The existing values name several broad outcomes but do not name these specific adopted or rejected design choices.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions combine or repeat decision questions. Dimension 10, "Replica Read Routing," mixes read selection with write quorum, replica count, and quorum-cost outcomes; move values 10.4 and 10.8–10.10 (and their related outcomes) to dimension 20, "Reference-Update Coordination," while retaining read-routing values in 10. Dimension 13, "Maintenance Execution Mode," combines initiation, compaction, expiration, and synchronous garbage-collection choices; split it into separate execution and compaction questions, keeping at least two existing alternatives in each. Dimension 11, "Maintenance Transition Safety," similarly mixes transition handling with checksum algorithms and repository-management policy; split the checksum choices 11.5 and 11.9–11.11 into their own question. Dimensions 9, "Replica Placement," and 19, "Repository Placement and Routing," overlap on where replicas are assigned; move the machine-placement alternatives 19.1, 19.5, and 19.6 to 9 and retain routing/rematerialization choices in 19. Finally, dimensions 8, "Repository Object Indexing and Storage," and 18, "Repository State Authority," overlap on storage representation: move storage alternatives such as 18.4 and 18.6–18.7 to 8, leaving 18 focused on authoritative versus cached state.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions use explicit question-like names and most values have concrete, distinguishable descriptions, such as 7.1 versus 7.2 and 17.1 versus 17.2. The main clarity problems are: dimension 1, "Replication Integration Layer," mixes update-replication mechanisms with repository-distribution mechanisms, and values 1.2/1.7 and 1.1/1.6 are difficult to distinguish; rename the dimension and clarify those value scopes. Value 2.5, "Consistency-and-partition priority," does not describe a repository freshness model like the other values in dimension 2; move it to dimension 20 or revise its placement. Dimension 11, "Maintenance Transition Safety," contains checksum and repository-management choices such as 11.5 and 11.9 that its transition-focused description does not cover; rename or reorganize the dimension so the question matches those values. Dimension 13, "Maintenance Execution Mode," similarly includes compaction algorithms and synchronous-GC outcomes, so its name and description should explicitly cover the existing execution and compaction alternatives.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the major decision areas implied by scaling Git across very many repositories, very large repositories, and very many users on both servers and clients. Server-side choices include replication and consistency (1, 2), placement and read routing (9, 10, 19), maintenance and compaction (11, 13, 17), storage authority (18), and coordinated reference updates (20), each with multiple candidate values. Client-side choices include working-tree population (6), change detection (7), object indexing and storage (8), maintenance scheduling (14), and remote synchronization (16), also with alternatives. Repository scale and hosting-model tradeoffs are represented by 15, while even narrower areas such as write continuity (12) provide more than one candidate. No major use-case area lacks a decision point with multiple candidates under the stated evaluation criterion.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions directly address scaling Git hosting or clients, including replication and consistency (1, 2, 9, 10, 17, 20), maintenance and failure handling (11–14), and large-repository client/storage techniques (6–8, 16, 18–19). The main scope weakness is dimension 15, "Repository Hosting Model": values 15.2 "Distributed repository model" and 15.3 "Offline distributed workflow" describe general Git workflow characteristics rather than architectural decisions specifically needed to scale very many repositories, large repositories, or users; drop dimension 15 or move only its centralized-hosting content into the hosting-placement dimensions. Value 6.11 "Source-directory repository placement" is also a narrow usage convention rather than a scaling decision; move it out of dimension 6 or drop it. Value 11.6 "Pet-style repository management" is an operational management characterization and only tangentially addresses the stated scaling architecture; move it to a repository lifecycle/operations dimension or drop it.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: The taxonomy largely avoids explicit catch-all buckets: there are no dimensions or values named Other, Miscellaneous, General, or Various. The main exception is value 8.12, "Server-side non-packfile representation," whose description covers any unspecified representation other than client-facing packfiles. Drop 8.12 or reorganize its specific alternatives into the existing repository-state-authority dimensions instead of retaining this open-ended bucket.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers both large-scale hosting and client scaling, but several dimensions combine distinct decision points rather than presenting one question with alternative answers. Split dimension 8, "Repository Object Indexing and Storage," into client index representation (8.1–8.6) and Git object storage/transfer (8.7–8.18). Restrict dimension 10, "Replica Read Routing," to read selection by moving replica counts and write-quorum choices (10.4, 10.8–10.10) to dimension 20, "Reference-Update Coordination." Split dimension 13, "Maintenance Execution Mode," by moving compaction choices (13.5–13.8) to dimension 17, "Compaction Coordination." Split dimension 6, "Working-Tree Population Strategy," so population choices remain there while cache deployment and client-distribution choices (6.5–6.7 and 6.11–6.13) are reorganized separately. Finally, keep dimension 18, "Repository State Authority," focused on authority location and move storage-format choices (18.4, 18.6, 18.7) to dimension 8; these changes remove substantial mixing of hosting, replication, maintenance, and client decisions.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many candidate-rich but question-mixed dimensions, so it only weakly satisfies the one-decision-point rule. Most importantly, dimension 20 (Reference-Update Coordination) mixes consensus/order, locking, commit protocol, durability, throughput targets, and performance effects; split these into separate questions while keeping at least two candidates in each. Dimension 8 (Repository Object Indexing and Storage) similarly combines index formats, object-storage choices, server-side representations, DAG traversal, and transfer mechanisms; split the existing values into coherent indexing, storage, and hosting/transfer decisions. Dimension 10 (Replica Read Routing) mixes read selection with replica counts, voting/quorum rules, and write thresholds; split routing from replication/quorum policy. Dimension 13 (Maintenance Execution Mode) combines execution/scheduling choices with pack compaction and garbage-collection strategies; split those groups. Dimension 6 (Working-Tree Population Strategy) combines population models, GVFS cache deployment, repository placement, and client distribution; split the alternatives and move the unrelated singleton 6.11 to the decision it answers. Other serious cases include dimension 1 mixing replication integration with distribution mechanisms, dimension 11 mixing maintenance transitions with checksum and repository-management policy, and dimension 16 whose 16.1, 16.2, and 16.3 are separate singleton decisions rather than alternatives to one question. Although many choices are grounded in relevant scale, latency, consistency, availability, and maintenance forces, the numerous mixed topics and singleton decision points require substantial reorganization.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses, and outcomes are generally described as effects rather than alternatives. However, dimension 1, "Replication Integration Layer," repeats overlapping candidates under conflicting statuses: 1.2 "Packfile-level replication" versus 1.7 "Packfile-level repository distribution," and 1.3 "Filesystem block-level replication" versus 1.6 "Filesystem-level repository distribution." Merge each overlapping pair or separate the decision dimensions so each candidate has one status. In dimension 10, "Replica Read Routing," 10.8 "Two-copy synchronous commitment" is accepted while 10.10 "Two-copy durability strategy" is rejected despite describing use of one additional copy as the strategy; merge these if they are the same candidate, or rewrite 10.10 to explicitly describe a declined option and distinguish it from 10.8.

criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers most adopted and rejected options across the Scalar and Spokes passages, including Git application-level replication (s02_p01), three-phase commit (s02_p03), quorum durability (s03_p02, s03_p09), quiescing and rolling reboots (s03_p07, s03_p08), background maintenance (s05_p09, s05_p11), sparse checkout and partial clone (s04_p02, s05_p04), and WAL/rendezvous-hashing designs (s01_p11). A few specific options are not explicitly named: add 'Git built-in filesystem monitor' to dimension 7, Working-Directory Change Detection, supported by s04_p02; add 'Atomic Git reference-update transactions' to dimension 28, Reference Update Ordering, supported by s02_p04; add 'Cone-mode sparse checkout' to dimension 38, Working-Tree Population Mode, supported by s05_p04; add 'Loose-object cleanup' to dimension 27, Maintenance Compaction Strategy, supported by s05_p12; and add 'Graceful server retirement with replica replenishment' to dimension 42, Server Reboot Maintenance Policy, supported by s03_p09.
